A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ALL research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original toy experiments, simulated AES experiments and evaluations on six real leakage datasets, including quantitative results in Tables 4–6.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and real-dataset evaluations, component ablations, sensitivity experiments and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendix E.

M1.justification: The constrained mutual-information objective and adversarial classifier/mask framework remain. V2 replaces the unbiased REBAR gradient estimator with biased CONCRETE at fixed temperature 1 (Section 4.2 and Appendix D.4), a localized but substantive change to the training procedure.

E1.justification: The six real datasets and four simulated AES perturbation scenarios remain. V1's separate mixed-order and redundant first-order toy experiments are replaced by a scenario combining redundancy with multiple second-order leaking pairs (v2 Section 5.1 and Appendix E.1), changing a limited part of the synthetic coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds actual evaluations of OccPOI, m-Occlusion and second-order m-Occlusion, including tuned-window variants, alongside the retained statistical and attribution baselines. V1 discussed the related Yap and Schamberger methods but did not benchmark them. These additions substantially expand comparison with closely related approaches.

E3.justification: V2 replaces oGMM agreement with an SNR-based oracle and adds template-attack evaluation using selected features. Training settings and selection procedures also change: supervised ASCAD training increases from 10k steps to 20k/40k, and ALL selection changes from reverse occlusion alone to a composite criterion. These are substantive protocol revisions, not merely additional documentation.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's toy demonstrations and synthetic parameter sweeps, v2 adds controlled ablations of heavy input dropout, cooperative versus adversarial training, mask conditioning and smoothing (Appendix E.3.7). It also adds real-data learning-rate and budget sensitivity analyses and hyperparameter-search distributions. The earlier joint synthetic budget sweeps are replaced by fixed-budget simulations.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark means and standard deviations over five seeds. V2 adds median, quartile and whisker summaries of hyperparameter-search outcomes (Figures 20–21) and explicitly describes error-bar-based grouping of best results. These extend statistical reporting without establishing an increase in repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Numerical results are extensively revised and expanded. For example, ALL's ASCAD-fixed reverse-occlusion score changes from 125.5 ± 0.4 in v1 Table 6 to 126.4 ± 0.2 in v2 Table 13. V2 additionally reports template-attack results, new toy outcomes, ablations and runtimes. Changed methods and settings prevent interpreting these as controlled version-to-version performance gains.

T1.justification: The main proposition and corollaries establishing the mutual-information formulation are retained from Appendix B.2 to D.2. V2 revises the conditional-information convergence argument using a bounded chain-rule sum, changes the gradient-estimator derivation to CONCRETE, and adds computational complexity bounds in Table 15. The central theoretical framework remains intact.

C1.justification: The central scientific contributions remain an information-theoretic definition of leakiness, ALL as its adversarial deep-learning approximation, and validation across AES, ECC and RSA implementations. Expanded comparisons and stronger descriptions of benchmark breadth support these retained contributions without materially changing their scientific scope.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands v1's scattered qualifications into explicit limitations of oracle assessments, DNN tests, template attacks, computational cost, tuning, synchronization and evaluation on cropped traces (Appendix F). New ablations also support interpretations concerning regularization, smoothing and the mixed usefulness of mask conditioning, materially refining explanations of ALL's gains and applicability.

D1.justification: V1 already supplied code access and hyperparameter tables. V2 adds ALL and evaluation pseudocode, a linked self-contained implementation, detailed comparator adaptations, dataset sizes and DPAv4/OTP processing disclosures, and A6000 runtime measurements. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although Algorithm 4's mask expression conflicts with its stated unocclusion convention.

R1.justification: Sections 3 and 4.3 and Appendix C substantially develop the relationship to prior methods, including their differing objectives and computational costs. Newly cited Egger et al. (2022) informs the white-box oracle and positioning of ALL as complementary to expert analysis. Yap and Schamberger were already cited in v1; their expanded treatment is not a new citation.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction, background, method explanation and experimental narrative, including a clearer attacker/defender explanation. It reorganizes the appendices around notation, background, related work, derivations, experiments and limitations. This exceeds renumbering or expansion solely through new scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column layout. V2 redraws the method and causal diagrams, adds notation and architecture displays, introduces a consolidated main results table, and substantially reorganizes experimental graphics. Many of v1's individual baseline and occlusion-curve grids are replaced by summary tables and diagnostic plots.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's validation by evaluating closely related methods and testing whether regularization, smoothing or particular ALL components explain the gains. Complementary attack evaluation, runtime measurements and explicit limitations substantially improve the evidence and its interpretation. The biased gradient relaxation, acknowledged comparator contamination and Algorithm 4's inconsistent mask convention remain drawbacks, but the expanded controls and transparency provide a substantial net improvement.
